splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on when actuarial assumptions must be finalized for purposes of calculating employer withdrawal liability under ERISA. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the end of the prior plan year, so long as they are applied to data as of that date.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be finalized by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and courts lack authority to create such a common-law doctrine extending punishment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: There is a longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prevents relitigating any previously presented claim — when bringing successive § 2255 motions, in addition to § 2255(h)'s separate requirements. The outcome determines whether federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, preventing them from relitigating any previously raised claim.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners filing § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. Some circuits grant candidates broad standing based on competitive injury, while others require more particularized harm. The outcome affects the ability to challenge mail-in voting rules, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate suffers a cognizable competitive injury from election laws that allegedly dilute lawful votes, giving them Article III standing to challenge such laws pre-election.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate must show more than a generalized competitive injury and must demonstrate particularized harm to establish Article III standing for pre-election challenges.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes precedence over deference to agency interpretations (Auer/Kisor deference) when construing ambiguous provisions that carry criminal consequences, including Sentencing Guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's or an agency's interpretation of an ambiguous guideline or regulation with criminal implications, or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of the defendant. This split has deepened after Loper Bright overruled Chevron and implicates fundamental questions about expanding criminal liability through delegated authority.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, preventing agencies from using delegated power to expand criminal liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference (including to Sentencing Commission commentary) takes precedence over the rule of lenity when interpreting ambiguous Guidelines enhancements or criminal regulations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines commentary (Application Note 1) can expand the definition of 'controlled substance offense' under U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) to include inchoate offenses such as conspiracy, attempt, and aiding and abetting, when the guideline text does not mention them.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2, which adds inchoate offenses to the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson, or whether it impermissibly expands the guideline text. This affects career-offender designations and can dramatically increase sentences.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and controlling
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is a valid, authoritative interpretation of the career-offender guideline and that inchoate offenses qualify as controlled substance offenses under § 4B1.2(b).

positions.label: Commentary impermissibly expands the guideline
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly adds to, rather than interprets, the guideline, so it is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to be met for disqualification) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), or whether possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. The split leads to dramatically different sentences for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on where they are prosecuted.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1), reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may expressly punish a defendant for violations of supervised release conditions, or whether revocation sentences must be limited to sanctioning the breach of trust.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit permits district courts to expressly punish defendants for the underlying conduct that violated supervised release, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split. Other circuits hold that revocation sentences should address the breach of the court's trust rather than punish the new conduct. This affects hundreds of supervised release revocations annually.

positions.label: Courts may punish for violations
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release conditions, not just for the breach of trust. Under United States v. Lewis, the Sixth Circuit permits punishment-based reasoning at revocation.

positions.label: Revocation sentences address breach of trust, not punishment
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of supervised release revocation is to sanction the breach of the court's trust, not to punish the defendant for the new criminal conduct that constituted the violation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) encompasses state drug convictions involving substances not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines when the state criminalizes a substance not on the federal schedule. Some circuits hold the Guidelines broadly reference state law offenses regardless of federal scheduling, while others require the substance to be federally controlled.

positions.label: State schedule controls — no federal-law limitation
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines includes offenses under state law regardless of whether the substance is controlled under federal law, because there is no textual basis to graft a federal law limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Federal schedule controls
positions.summary: Holds that a prior state conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance at issue is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

circuits.name: First Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. De La Rosa

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law, such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c), can serve as an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether non-retroactive changes in law can contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for a sentence reduction under the compassionate release statute. This split has deepened as the Sentencing Commission adopted a policy statement (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) attempting to authorize such reductions, with some circuits rejecting the Commission's authority to do so.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons under § 3582(c)(1)(A), as allowing such relief would circumvent Congress's decision not to make the change retroactive.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law may be considered, alone or in combination with other factors, as extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction, particularly after the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement explicitly authorized such consideration.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor when a Chapter 13 case is converted in good faith to Chapter 7.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A). This has significant practical consequences for debtors whose property values increase during their Chapter 13 plan.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the broad scope of § 541(a) means post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, as 'property of the estate as of the date of filing' encompasses the property's full value including later appreciation.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) protects good-faith converting debtors by limiting the estate to the property's value at the time of the original filing, meaning post-petition appreciation remains with the debtor.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil appeal deadline (60 days for government cases) or the criminal appeal deadline (14 days) applies to appeals from orders denying attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal proceeding or part of the criminal case itself, which determines the applicable appeal deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline (30 or 60 days) governs the time to appeal.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that Hyde Amendment fee motions arise from and are part of the criminal case, so the shorter criminal appeal deadline applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner challenging conditions or terms of confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed via habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241 or may bring a civil rights action, and whether habeas is the exclusive remedy for BOP decisions affecting the timing of release.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether challenges to BOP decisions — such as denial of First Step Act earned time credits for transfer to prerelease custody — must be brought as habeas petitions or may be brought as civil rights actions. The distinction matters because habeas requires exhaustion and limits remedies, while civil rights claims offer broader relief. The Eighth Circuit has acknowledged the 'unresolved conflict' spanning more than half a century.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for release-timing claims
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's claim effectively challenges the duration or timing of confinement, including BOP decisions about earned time credits and prerelease custody, habeas corpus is the sole federal remedy.

positions.label: Civil rights actions may be available for conditions claims
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens or § 1983) to challenge conditions and terms of confinement, even when the relief sought might incidentally affect release timing, as habeas is required only for challenges to the fact or duration of confinement.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine as an order effectively unreviewable on appeal from final judgment.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of 'high order' warranting immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine, noting the strong interest in medical privacy. Other circuits have not uniformly recognized such orders as immediately appealable, creating potential disagreement on the scope of the collateral order doctrine for privacy-related sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of high order that would be irreparably lost if review were delayed until final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are not immediately appealable because the harm from disclosure can be partially remedied on appeal and does not meet the collateral order doctrine's stringent requirements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a trademark owner asserting a likelihood of confusion must demonstrate that consumers are likely to be confused at the time of purchase, or whether post-sale confusion is sufficient to support a trademark infringement claim.
splits.description: The circuits disagree on whether post-sale confusion — confusion experienced by third-party observers after a purchase is complete — can independently support a trademark infringement claim, or whether the confusion must occur at the point of sale. This affects how broadly trademark rights can be enforced against look-alike products.

positions.label: Post-sale confusion is sufficient
positions.summary: Holds that post-sale confusion among third-party observers can independently support a trademark infringement claim, even if purchasers are not confused at the point of sale.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Levi Strauss & Co. v. Blue Bell, Inc.

positions.label: Point-of-sale confusion required
positions.summary: Holds that confusion must be likely at the time of purchase to support a trademark infringement claim, and post-sale confusion alone is insufficient.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Checkpoint Systems, Inc. v. Check Point Software Technologies, Inc.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have applied different standards for evaluating discrimination claims against business operators, creating uncertainty about liability and available remedies in hospitality, retail, and service industries. SCOTUS granted cert to resolve the disagreement.

positions.label: Broader liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more expansive standard for establishing discrimination claims against business establishments, allowing broader theories of liability and damages.

positions.label: Narrower liability standard
positions.summary: Applies a more restrictive standard requiring stronger proof of discriminatory intent or conduct before imposing liability on business operators.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
